historical_timeline.summary: Born at Nine Mile, Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica.
Converts to Rastafari; his music career is under way.
Notices a pigmented lesion under the right great toenail, thought to be a football injury; sees two physicians.
Biopsy shows acral lentiginous melanoma; declines amputation; nail bed excision with a skin graft.
Collapses while jogging in New York; the melanoma has spread to the brain, lungs and liver; last concert two days later.
Radiation therapy in New York, then treatment at a clinic in Bavaria.
Dies in Miami at 36, after a flight home is diverted.
Remembered as the public face of acral melanoma in people with skin of color.

claims.statement: Robert Nesta Marley was born on February 6, 1945, at Nine Mile in Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica, the son of a Jamaican mother and a white English father.

source_links.locator: Early life: born at Nine Mile, Saint Ann Parish
son of a Jamaican mother and a white English father

claims.statement: He was a Jamaican singer, songwriter and musician, considered one of the pioneers of reggae, who toured the world with his band, the Wailers.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His work as a performing musician anchors the modern social history.

claims.statement: He was raised a Roman Catholic and converted to Rastafari in the late 1960s; he became known as a Rastafarian icon who infused his music with spirituality.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His faith is part of who he is; the modern episode records it as he would describe it and asks how it bears on his decisions.

source_links.locator: converted to Rastafari in the late 1960s

claims.statement: In 1977 he noticed a pigmented lesion on the nail bed of his right great toe and thought it was the result of a football injury. The first physician he saw thought that a reasonable explanation; because the lesion was growing, he saw a second physician, who performed a biopsy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the presenting problem: a pigmented nail lesion put down to trauma. A bruise under the nail grows out with the nail; a band that persists or widens needs a biopsy.

source_links.locator: lesion on the nail bed of his right great toe; football injury; two physicians
a dark spot under his toenail, attributed to a soccer injury
originally thought to be a sports injury

claims.statement: In July 1977 he was diagnosed with acral lentiginous melanoma of the right great toe, presenting as a pigmented lesion under the nail.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented disease to which the synthetic diagnosis is linked. Its thickness and stage were not made public.

source_links.locator: first diagnosed with ALM in July 1977

claims.statement: His doctors advised amputation of the toe, which he declined. Instead the nail and nail bed and the cancerous tissue were removed, and the area was covered with skin from his thigh.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented choice of a less extensive operation. Whether amputation would have cured him cannot be known.

source_links.locator: opted for excisional surgery, removing the nail bed and cancerous tissue
refused and opted for less invasive solutions

claims.statement: The sources give his reasons for declining amputation in different words: one reports that he said it would be against his Rastafari faith, another that his Rastafarian beliefs prohibited it, and an encyclopedia article that he cited religious beliefs and that amputation would have hindered his performing career.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His reasons are recorded only as these sources give them. The record makes no general statement about what the Rastafari faith permits, and it does not treat his faith as the cause of his death.

source_links.locator: he said it would be against his Rastafari faith
which would have hindered his performing career, citing religious beliefs

claims.statement: Whether the football injury caused the lesion is disputed: an encyclopedia article states that the lesion was not caused by the injury but was a sign of a cancer already present, and clinicians note that many people with acral melanoma recall an injury to the site, while the role of trauma is not established.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective reading. The modern episode treats the injury as the reason the lesion was first dismissed, not as its cause.

source_links.locator: many patients describe a history of trauma to the affected area
The underlying cause is not well defined

claims.statement: He continued to tour. In September 1980 he collapsed while jogging in Central Park, New York, and was found to have cancer that had spread to his brain, lungs and liver; his last concert was in Pittsburgh two days later.

source_links.locator: metastasized to his lungs, brain, and liver

claims.statement: He was treated at cancer centers including Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where he received radiation therapy, and then at the clinic of Josef Issels in Bavaria, Germany.
On a flight home to Jamaica his condition worsened, the flight was diverted to Miami, and he died at Cedars of Lebanon Hospital in Miami on May 11, 1981, at 36.

source_links.locator: died at the age of 36 of metastatic disease in May 1981

claims.statement: He has long served as the posthumous public face of skin cancer in people with skin of color; acral lentiginous melanoma is the most common melanoma in people of color, and awareness campaigns in his memory urge everyone to check their palms, soles, and nails.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His legacy in awareness, which the modern self-examination teaching reflects.

source_links.locator: posthumous poster child for skin cancer in people with skin of color

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Diagnose acral melanoma promptly in a 32-year-old Black man whose dark toenail band was first put down to a football injury: recognize the warning signs of nail melanoma (a band wider than 3 mm, irregular in color and spacing, that does not grow out, with pigment on the nail fold), use dermoscopy, and obtain a full-thickness nail matrix biopsy within the week; stage by AJCC 8th edition and offer sentinel lymph node biopsy for a T1b melanoma; plan surgery with a surgical oncologist through a documented shared decision that sets out amputation and digit-sparing excision of the whole nail unit, chooses digit-sparing surgery where it is oncologically appropriate, and respects his values and his faith; decide on adjuvant therapy by stage; set up surveillance; and teach skin self-examination of the palms, soles, between the toes and all the nails, the sites people with darker skin most need to check, on the NCCN cutaneous melanoma guideline, the AAD primary melanoma guideline, and the ASCO-SSO sentinel node guideline.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Marley returns nine days after his first visit. The clinic's dermatologist examined the nail with dermoscopy two days after that visit, found a band with irregular lines of varying color and spacing and pigment on the nail fold, and took a full-thickness excisional biopsy of the nail matrix under a digital block. The biopsy shows acral lentiginous melanoma, 0.8 mm thick, not ulcerated. The biopsy site has healed under the dressing; he has needed no pain medicine. He has no lumps in the groin or behind the knee, no cough, headache, or weight loss. Dr. Mbeki-Rowe of surgical oncology saw him this morning and went through the choices for surgery with him at length. He said that his faith, his music and his football all matter to him in this decision, and that he would like to keep the toe if that can be done without lowering his chance of cure. He has had no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment_plan.display: Acral lentiginous melanoma of the right great toe nail unit, clinical stage IB (cT1b N0 M0)
assessment_plan.assessment: A thin acral melanoma of the nail unit, diagnosed nine days after he first came in, because a band that had not grown out and pigment on the nail fold were biopsied rather than called a bruise. Acral melanoma is the most common melanoma in people with darker skin and is not caused by the sun. At 0.8 mm it is T1b: no scans or blood tests are needed, and a sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered because the chance of a positive node is about 5 to 10 percent. Dr. Mbeki-Rowe set out the two surgical choices: amputation of the toe at the interphalangeal joint, or digit-sparing excision of the whole nail unit down to the bone with a skin graft. For a melanoma this thin, digit-sparing excision is an accepted choice with similar survival in published series, at the cost of a higher chance of a local recurrence that would then need amputation. With his values in view, he chose digit-sparing excision with a sentinel node biopsy, and agreed in advance that amputation would be the next step if the margins were involved or the melanoma proved thicker
plan: Digit-sparing excision of the nail unit with a full-thickness skin graft and right inguinal sentinel node biopsy with Dr. Mbeki-Rowe in two weeks, after lymphoscintigraphy the same morning

hpi.narrative: Mr. Marley returns two weeks after digit-sparing en bloc excision of the nail unit of his right great toe, with a full-thickness skin graft from the inner upper arm and a right inguinal sentinel node biopsy, as a day case. The tie-over dressing came off at one week and the graft had taken. He took acetaminophen for nine days and needs nothing now. He walks in the stiff-soled postoperative shoe and has kept the foot raised when resting. The groin wound is comfortable, with no swelling. The final pathology is back. He has had no thoughts of self-harm.

Surveillance is by history and examination, with no routine scans or blood tests

hpi.narrative: Mr. Marley returns for his first melanoma surveillance visit, about three and a half months after digit-sparing excision of a stage IA acral melanoma of the right great toe. The graft is fully healed, and he runs and plays football without pain; he still wears the ankle support for football since the sprain eight weeks ago, which has healed. He has examined his skin and nails each month with a mirror and photographed the graft; he has seen no change. His HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests from the preventive visit were negative, with no immunity to hepatitis B, and he is due the second hepatitis B vaccine. He leaves on tour next week. He has had no thoughts of self-harm.

referral.question: Suspected subungual melanoma of the right great toe in a 32-year-old musician and footballer with dark skin: a brown-black band about 5 mm wide that has not grown out in two months, with pigment on the proximal nail fold. A full-thickness nail matrix biopsy is booked with our dermatologist this week. Please see him with the result to advise on staging and definitive surgery
referral.urgency: Urgent, within two weeks, with the biopsy result
referral.pertinent_history: He noticed the dark stripe about two months ago after a knock at football and was told at an urgent care clinic a month ago that it was a bruise. It has not grown out with the nail and the color has spread onto the skin at the base of the nail. The toe is barely sore. Examination: a brown-black longitudinal band about a third of the nail wide, with irregular dark lines, and pigment on the proximal nail fold (Hutchinson sign); the nail plate is intact; no nodule or ulcer; no popliteal or inguinal nodes. Fitzpatrick type VI skin. Otherwise well; no medicines; no known allergies; does not smoke tobacco. He tours as a musician, runs and plays football several times a week, and his Rastafari faith is central to how he makes decisions. He wants a clear explanation and time to decide about any treatment, and he decides who is told about his health

Should he be offered a sentinel lymph node biopsy?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Marley, 32, is seen at the request of Dr. Clarke with the result of a nail matrix biopsy taken two days after his first visit. He noticed a dark band in his right great toenail about two months ago after a knock at football; it did not grow out, and pigment spread onto the nail fold. He is otherwise well, takes no medicines, and has had no previous operations. He is a touring musician who runs and plays football several times a week. He told me that his faith, his music and his football all matter to him in this decision, and that he would like to keep the toe if that can be done without lowering his chance of cure
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Clarke's intake note. Dermoscopy by the clinic's dermatologist: a brown-black band about 5 mm wide with longitudinal lines irregular in color, thickness and spacing, and pigment on the proximal nail fold and hyponychium. Full-thickness excisional nail matrix biopsy: acral lentiginous melanoma, Breslow thickness 0.8 mm, not ulcerated, mitotic rate 1 per mm2, no lymphovascular or perineural invasion, no microsatellites, with melanoma in situ at the lateral edges of the specimen

exam.finding: Biopsy site healing over the proximal nail; the distal part of the band remains in the nail plate; pigment on the proximal nail fold; no nodule or ulcer
No right popliteal or inguinal nodes; no left inguinal, axillary, or cervical nodes
No other suspicious lesion on the skin, palms, soles, or nails

assessment.display: Acral lentiginous melanoma of the right great toe nail unit, clinical stage IB (cT1b N0 M0)
assessment.assessment: A thin invasive acral melanoma of the nail unit, T1b by the AJCC 8th edition because it is 0.8 mm thick, with no clinical sign of spread: clinical stage IB. No scans or blood tests are needed at this stage. The chance that a sentinel node contains melanoma is about 5 to 10 percent, so a sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered; it gives the most accurate stage, which decides whether treatment after surgery would be considered. There are two surgical choices. Amputation at the interphalangeal joint has the lowest chance of the melanoma returning in the toe. Digit-sparing en bloc excision of the whole nail unit down to the bone, with a 5 to 10 mm margin and a full-thickness skin graft, keeps the toe and its function; for melanomas this thin, published series show similar survival, with a higher chance (in some series about one in five) of a local recurrence that would then be treated by amputation. Either is oncologically appropriate for him; it is his decision, and his wish to keep the toe for his faith, his music and his football is a sound reason to choose the digit-sparing operation. If the excision showed a thicker melanoma or involved margins, I would recommend amputation. Adjuvant immunotherapy is considered only from stage IIB, so it is not expected to be needed unless the sentinel node is positive

recommendations: Lymphoscintigraphy and right inguinal sentinel lymph node biopsy, with the definitive operation, in two weeks

Definitive surgery by his choice: digit-sparing en bloc excision of the nail unit down to the bone with a 5 to 10 mm margin and a full-thickness skin graft from the inner upper arm; amputation at the interphalangeal joint if the margins are involved or the melanoma proves thicker
No staging CT, PET, or LDH for clinical stage IB without symptoms; no blood tests needed before surgery

No adjuvant therapy if the sentinel node is negative; surveillance with history and examination of the skin, nails, graft and nodes every 6 to 12 months for 5 years and then yearly, with a yearly full skin examination by dermatology
Monthly skin self-examination, including the palms, soles, between the toes and all nails, the graft, and both groins, taught after surgery
A stiff-soled shoe until the graft heals, then a graded return to running and football
